newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rookie Telekom shareholders feast on food and fun.
newsitem.headline: Rookie Telekom shareholders feast on food and fun.

text.p: Grey-haired grannies and acne-faced teenagers mingled with suburban housewives and bearded labourers at Deutsche Telekom's first public shareholder meeting on Thursday.

There were plenty of bankers in smart double-breasted suits at one of the largest shareholder meetings in German history as well, but the grey investor class that usually dominates shareholder meetings was clearly in the minority.

"It's totally awesome to make so much money by doing absolutely nothing," said Matthias Walz, a 21-year-old student who bought 50 shares in November that are now worth 1,000 marks ($580) more. "I like this shareholder business."

Walz and more than 10,000 mostly happy Telekom shareholders packed Frankfurt's cavernous convention centre for the meeting. Telekom officials said it was probably the biggest gathering of first-time shareholders in German history.

"They've put together an excellent show," said Georg Hauser, a 51-year-old farmer and first-time shareholder who travelled some eight hours from Fuessen in the Bavarian Alps. "I've never seen so many friendly people and such perfect organisation."

Wearing a bright purple suit and pink shirt, Hauser said he was delighted his 170 Telekom shares had risen so much in value since the flotation in November. He has since become an avid reader of the financial section of his local newspaper.

"The adviser at my bank had urged me to sell my shares when the price hit 33 marks, but I had a feeling I should keep them," Hauser said, a proud smile spreading across his weathered face. Telekom shares, launched at 28.50 marks, are now worth 42.50 marks.
Telekom's flotation in November was the largest in European history. A total of 713 million shares were sold to 1.9 million investors, about one-third of whom became shareholders for the first time.
The company said before the meeting it had also reached agreement with the government to allow Bonn to sell a further 25 percent of Telekom's capital to strategic investors.
Since November's flotation, the share price has climbed nearly 50 percent.
"You can't complain about that," said Albert Leyendecker, 70-year-old retired welder wearing a white sweater and matching trousers. "I never thought the share would do that well."

Inge Krois, a 46-year-old merchant from the northern town of Paderborn, said she had emptied her savings account to buy Telekom shares and regretted she hadn't become a stock market investor sooner because the return on savings was so paltry.
But Krois said her favourite part of her first shareholder meeting was making some new friends.

"I've met some very nice people here today," Krois said while sipping a cup of coffee with two other women in a snack area while Telekom chairman Ron Sommer's speech was relayed on television screens in the background.
"I wanted to see what a shareholder meeting was like," she said. "It has been a delightful social event."

The neophyte shareholders listened quietly as Sommer and supervisory board chairman Helmut Sihler patiently explained how the shareholder meeting worked. They were warned not to smoke or take pictures in the main hall or in the three auxiliary halls set up to accommodate the rock-concert-sized crowd.
"I've never seen so many people in my life," said a retired civil servant clad in lederhosen who said his name was Peter.
Michael Hartung, a 37-year-old wearing blue jeans with holes and long unruly hair, admitted he never envisioned himself owning stocks and becoming a full-blooded capitalist.
"It's an interesting experience," said the bearded technician from Cologne.
Telekom had expected about 17,000 shareholders to attend. Only chemical giant Bayer, which once had 25,000 at a meeting, and Daimler-Benz, have gatherings of the same dimension.
Christian Koenig, an 18-year-old student from Hanau near Frankfurt, was enjoying the free bratwurst and potato salad lunch as he explained why he had bought Telekom shares.

"I inherited some money from my grandfather," Koenig said shyly. "But I intend to sell the shares in about four weeks and invest the money elsewhere. Telekom will be facing some tough competition soon and I think it's time to sell." $ = 1.725 German Marks)
